title: How to register as a voter
summary: Who qualifies, what to carry, and where to go to get onto the voters' roll.
body: You qualify to register if you are a Kenyan citizen, are 18 years or older, and hold a national ID card or a valid Kenyan passport.

Registration is done in person at your constituency's IEBC office or at any gazetted registration centre during a registration drive. The clerk captures your details and fingerprints using a BVR (Biometric Voter Registration) kit.
You choose the polling centre where you will vote. Pick one close to where you actually live: that is where you must show up on election day.
Registration is free. Nobody may charge you, and nobody may register on your behalf.
After registering you receive an acknowledgement slip. Keep it, but note that the slip is not required to vote; your ID or passport is what you present on election day.

title: What documents do you need?
summary: The national ID or passport rule, and what to do if you have neither yet.
body: Only two documents can be used to register and to vote: your Kenyan national identity card or a valid Kenyan passport. Waiting-card slips, birth certificates, driving licences and student IDs are not accepted.

If you have never had an ID, apply at your nearest Huduma Centre or chief's office as early as possible. Processing can take weeks, and you cannot register as a voter until you hold the physical document.
If your ID is lost, apply for a replacement immediately. You can register with a passport in the meantime if you hold one.
The name and details on the register must match your document. If you have changed your name, sort the ID record out first.

title: Checking your registration status
summary: Confirm you are on the roll, at the right polling station, before the deadline.
body: Do not assume you are registered because you registered once years ago. Registers are cleaned up, and details can be wrong. Check early so there is time to fix problems.

You can verify by SMS: send your national ID number to the IEBC short code (70000 in past elections; confirm the current code on iebc.or.ke). The reply shows your registration details and polling station.
You can also verify online through the IEBC voter verification portal, or in person at your constituency's IEBC office.

If your details are wrong, or you want to transfer to a different polling station, visit the constituency IEBC office before the register inspection window closes. Transfers are not possible in the final months before the election.

title: The six ballots you cast
summary: President, Governor, Senator, Woman Rep, MP and MCA: what each one does.
body: On election day you receive six ballot papers, each a different colour, and you vote for six different seats.
President: head of state and government, elected nationally. A winner needs over half of all votes cast nationally plus at least 25% of votes in at least 24 counties.
Governor: heads your county government, running county services like health facilities, county roads, water, and markets.
Senator: represents your county in the Senate, which protects county interests and oversees how counties spend money.
Woman Representative: your county's elected woman member of the National Assembly, with a focus on promoting the interests of women and youth.
Member of Parliament (MP): represents your constituency in the National Assembly, which makes national laws and approves the national budget.
Member of County Assembly (MCA): represents your ward in the county assembly, which makes county laws and oversees the governor. This is the leader closest to your daily life.
You may vote for candidates from different parties on different ballots. Each ballot is independent.

title: Election day, step by step
summary: What happens from the queue to the ballot box, and your rights in the polling station.
body: Polls typically open at 6am and close at 5pm. Anyone in the queue by closing time is allowed to vote, however long it takes.
Carry the document you registered with: your national ID or passport. Nothing else is needed.
At the desk, an official checks your identity against the electronic register (KIEMS kit), usually by fingerprint.
You receive six ballot papers. In the booth, mark ONE candidate per ballot with a clear mark inside that candidate's box. Fold each paper and drop it into the matching-colour ballot box.
Voting is secret. Nobody, including officials, party agents, or family, may watch you mark your ballot or ask afterwards who you voted for.
It is illegal for anyone to pay you, transport you in exchange for your vote, or campaign inside or near a polling station. Report violations to the presiding officer or the police.

title: How votes are counted
summary: Counting happens at your polling station, in the open, before results move up the chain.
body: Counting starts at the polling station immediately after polls close, in front of party agents and observers. Ballots never leave the station uncounted.

For each of the six elections, ballots are sorted per candidate, counted, and the totals entered on a results form signed by officials and agents. A copy is posted at the station's door for anyone to photograph.
Presidential results forms (Form 34A) are transmitted electronically to the constituency and national tallying centres, alongside the physical forms.
The station-level form is the primary record. Every total announced later must trace back to those forms, which is why they are public.
Disputes go to the courts: election petitions for most seats, and the Supreme Court for the presidency, within strict timelines.

title: Spoilt and rejected votes
summary: The difference between the two, and how to make sure your vote counts.
body: A REJECTED vote is a ballot that cannot be counted for any candidate: it is blank, marked for more than one candidate, or marked so unclearly that the intention is not obvious. Rejected ballots are recorded but count for nobody.
A SPOILT ballot is one you spoil by mistake BEFORE casting it. Take it back to the presiding officer: you are entitled to have it cancelled and to receive a fresh ballot paper.
To make your vote count: use the pen provided, make one clear mark (a tick or an X) inside one candidate's box, don't write anything else on the paper, and don't sign it.
If you are unsure, ask the polling officials to explain the marking rules before you enter the booth. They may explain the process, but never who to vote for.

title: Your rights as a voter
summary: Assistance, accessibility, secrecy, and what nobody is allowed to do to you.
body: You have the right to register and vote without paying anyone, without intimidation, and without disclosing your choice to anyone.

If you are unable to mark the ballot yourself due to disability or literacy, you may be assisted by a person of your choice, or by the presiding officer in the presence of agents. Your choice remains confidential.
Persons with disabilities, pregnant women, nursing mothers and the elderly are entitled to priority in the queue.
Your employer must allow you reasonable time to vote. Election day is a public holiday.
Nobody may buy your vote, threaten you over it, or force you to attend a rally. Voter bribery and intimidation are crimes. Report them to the IEBC, the police, or the EACC.
You have the right to accurate information. Check claims against official IEBC communications, and be wary of unsourced forwards on social media.
